messages.subject: predictions + functions of predictions
messages.body_plain:
Hi INLA group,
I have a couple questions about computing the predictions and functions of predictions.Here is what I have figured out to get some predictions:

# simulate some poisson data
n = 20
x = rnorm(n)
lambda = exp(2 + x +  rnorm(n,sd=0.02))
y = rpois(n, lambda)
y.true <- y

# set some values for  predictions
y[15:20] <- NA
mod.inla = inla(y ~ x, data = data.frame(x,y), family="poisson", control.predictor = list(compute=TRUE))
summary(mod.inla)
y.hat <- mod.inla$summary.fitted.values$mean

# predicted values for NAs use identity link function so we need to transform it using the inverse of the link function
y.pred <- y.hat
for (i in 15:20){
y.pred[i] <- inla.expectation(function(x) exp(x), mod.inla$marginals.fitted.values[[i]])
}
plot(y.pred, y.true)

My questions are:
1. I think this is how to get predictions for this simple poisson model but I would like to confirm that I am doing the right thing.
2. How to get functions of the predictions with the CORRECT CI? For example, if I want to compute (y.pred[17]+y.pred[18])/y.pred[17], is there a way to get the CI in inla?

Many thanks!

Cici

messages.subject: Re: A-matrix feature
messages.body_plain:
When using the A matrix, the most common mistakes I've made are indexing errors.  If the results look like they've been shuffled around a bit, you should check those!

The problem with the intercept is a bit tricky to explain, but I'll do my best.  What I'm going to describe is a simple version of what the inla.stack() function does, and I suggest that you always use that (instead of programming it yourself), as it's less error prone!

Assume you have a model like  y ~ 1 + height + f(space, model="rw2"), where the covariate height is measured at the data locations (which are NOT on the lattice) and the rw2 effect (space) is specified on a lattice.  You then use an A matrix to link the value of the effect 'space' on the lattice to the interpolated value at the data location.  Because you only want the A matrix to apply  to 'space', you need to be a bit careful.

(NB:: This is an explanation of what would be done naively and does NOT deal with the intercept properly.  See note at end!)

Step 1:  Pad everything with NAs.  Because we have to sections of the problem (the bit on the lattice and the bit off the lattice), we need to separate them somehow.  In R-INLA, we do this by adding NAs to the covariates (and effect indicies) to indicate which bits we want to be ignored.  Keeping with the order of the formula, we will put the off lattice effects (i.e. the covariates) first, and the lattice effects ('space') second.  Set height2 = c(height, rep(NA,length(space)) and space2 = c(rep(NA, length(space)), space).  This makes sure both vectors are of the same length, but have no 'overlapping' components.  The new formula is then y ~ 1 + height2 + f(space2, model = "rw2).

Step 2: Combine the A matrices.   We have two effects of two different sizes (one the length of the data and one the number of nodes in the spatial effect).  To combine them, we need to put two A matrices together.  The first one is an identity matrix (henceforth called Id)  with the same number of rows as the number of data points, and the second one is the matrix linking the spatial effect to the data (which we will call 'Aspace').  Then the combined A matrix stacks these columnwise against each other and the command is control.predictor = list(A = cBind(Id, Aspace) ).  (NB: The capital B in cBind makes sure the result is still a sparse matrix!!)

THE PROBLEM:  The problem is that the default intercept behaviour is (necessarily) stupid and CAN  NOT know that the latent effect has been split with NAs and therefore is of the form c(rep(1, length(height)), rep(1, length(space))).  That is, BOTH A MATRICES WILL PICK UP THE INTERCEPT AND IT WILL APPEAR TWICE! (It's actually worse than this, if the rows of Aspace dont' sum to one, it's impossible to interpret what the actual model is fitting!)

THE SOLUTION: The problem would not exist if instead of a massive vector of ones, the default intercept translated to c( rep(1, length(height)), rep(NA, length(space)) ).  As R cannot know this (an let us all pause to reflect on the stupidity of an automatic default intercept!), we need to do it  ourself.  So we set intercept=o c( rep(1, length(height)), rep(NA, length(space)) ) and make the formula
     y~ intercept + height + f(space, model="rw2)-1

I hope this explanation helped.  As you can see, this will not occur every single time you use the A matrix and a formula, but when it does, it can be devastating.  The best solution is to never rely on the default intercept, but the best that we can do is put a strong warning in the code that something may have gone terribly terribly wrong.

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Re: A-matrix feature
messages.body_plain:
Ah!  Ok.   That's my fault - I chose the parameter values poorly.

The problem is that the estimated spatial scale of the problem (and the TRUE scale of the simulated problem) is larger than the domain.  In this case, the field is essentially intrinsic and it's difficult to separate the non-zero mean of the posterior spatial effect from the intercept.  If you run the model with a larger value of kappa, it will work fine!

In this case, using the default intercept is not a mistake as there are no covariates/effects at different spatial locations.

/D

messages.subject: 2 steps BYM model: is it possible?
messages.subject_clean: 2 steps BYM model: is it possible?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all,

I would like to carry out a 2 steps spatial model, but I don’t know if it is possible with INLA.

First step:

I want to make a BYM model where I am smoothing a variable (a percentage).

                n~binomial(p,m)

                logit(p)=alpha+spatial+heterogeneous

                with these model we obtain p’, which are the posterior predictive distributions for each area (i.e. spatial smoothed percentages).

Second step:

I want to introduce the posterior predictive distributions as a covariate in another BYM model. I don’t want to introduce the posterior mean of p’ (or another point estimation). I would like to maintain the uncertainty (or variability) of these estimations and incorporate it into the following model.

                Therefore the model more or less:

                O~poisson(E·RR)

                Log(RR)=alpha+spatial+heterogeneous+beta·p’

Finally I would like to obtain the association, i.e. exp(beta) posterior mean and its credible interval.

Thank you for your help!

Marc

messages.subject_clean: models with more than one type of likelihood AND an observation matrix
messages.body_plain:
The r-inla program doesn't parse the A matrix and passes it to the C program "as is". So you need to use identity matrices (sparse matrices with ones on the diagonal) instead of NAs.  Otherwise, what you've done is correct - these two features work well together.  You can also use the inla.stack command, which should cover these cases.

Best wishes

Dan

messages.subject: Re: 2 steps BYM model: is it possible?
messages.subject_clean: 2 steps BYM model: is it possible?
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

The r-inla software cannot handle joint estimation of these kinds of models, since they cannot be (jointly) written on the standard generalised linear regression form (because of the logit-link for p; if the model had beta*logit(p) it could be done with current r-inla).  But they fall under a more general class of "two-stage models" for which it is perhaps possible to construct a general Laplace approximation method, extending the INLA method.

/Finn

messages.subject: Re: Question about Kronecker product models
messages.body_plain:
Hi Jonas,

we have used the Kronecker product models not in the SPDE context but for correlating smoothing priors
or overdispersion parameters, see http://arxiv.org/abs/1108.0606. We specified for example a random
walk over time for each of several geographical regions and then correlated them based on a Kronecker product
of a uniform correlation matrix and the structure matrix of the random walk.  This was useful on
one side to get more precise estimates and on the other side to improve the imputation of data missing
in one geographical region. We implemented this feature in INLA using the group-ing option. The R-code used
for the paper is posted on http://lib.stat.cmu.edu/aoas/498/. However, I will also try to
post a simple example on the r-inla website.

Hope this helps.

Best regards
Andrea

messages.subject: Re: Question about Kronecker product models
messages.body_plain:
Further to what Andrea said, there are currently only two models that can be used in Kronecker models: the exchangeable model and the AR(1) model.  I've used  SPDE \otimes AR(1) as a space-time model, but in principle it will work with any "left hand" latent model (BYM, RW2, etc).  An example is in the paper by Cameletti et al, which is in the "Papers" section.

To the best of my knowledge, there are plans for a general Kronecker product mechanism in INLA, however this has not been started yet.

Best,

Dan

messages.subject: Re: off grid on real line
messages.body_plain:
Hi!

Since the LGCP/SPDE construction is done through "clever" use of the observation matrix feature (control.predictor(A=...)) one can in principle apply it to any of the one-dimensional models on the real line, such as "rw2".

I am also adding wrapper functions to construct SPDE models on the real line, with "1D-mesh" objects to help with the book-keeping.  This experimental feature can be found in functions currently containing the name "inla.mesh.1d".  I think the only really missing link to using nearly identical code to the one for the triangulated meshes in the paper is the wrapper function for constructing the SPDE model object for a one-dimensional mesh, or to add support for this in the inla.spde2.matern wrapper.  I hope to have this fully implemented and documented in late February or March.

Later, we hope to have more user-friendly LGCP-wrappers around the basic SPDE-wrappers; some of this already exists but is not fully documented yet.

/Finn

messages.subject: Re: off grid on real line
messages.body_plain:
Hi Julia,

>I received also comment about using GMRF but I am actually interested in the continuous part: GRF. I don't understand why one could use rw2 in principle.

The RW2 model in 1D implements the continuous model found in Lindgren and Rue 2008 (from SJS). This was a prototype of the models more fully described in Lindgren, Rue and Lindström (2011) that used piecewise linear basis functions and the finite element method to construct a GMRF approximation to the continuous GRF.  So if you construct an "A matrix" yourself (or possibly use the experimental code - I don't know the details of that, sorry), you can use an intrinsic model in 1D with alpha=2.

> I thought the point of the SPDE solution is that it worked for the Matern class and the simplest on 1 D I could think off is the Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process.

The important distinction here is the SPDE *model*, which work with the Matern class, and the SPDE *code* in INLA, which is currently only implemented fully in 2D.  As Finn said above, we are getting to it, but it isn't done yet.  Unfortunately, with a project of this size, we have to build the code "as needed" (or at least "in order of priority").

Best wishes,

Dan

messages.subject: Re: off grid on real line
messages.body_plain:
Short reply: the rw2 (on R) is a special case of the Matern models (SPDE with alpha=2, kappa=0).  Ornstein-Uhlenbeck is another special case (alpha=1, kappa>0). rw1 corresponds to alpha=1, kappa=0.  The key to the LGCP models, regardless of which GRF model is used lies in the continuous space/time interpretation.  That the calculations are carried out using GMRFs can be viewed as just a computational implementation detail. (An important detail, but detail nonetheless...)
/Finn

I havn't heard about model averaging using DIC, but if there is some
kind of justification of it, I would be curious to know. [ The DIC does
not have a proper justification itself, so I am not very optimistic. ]

There is one paper that came to mind, I think they use AIC (and not DIC)
in the same manner,

S.P. Brooks, N. Friel, and R. King. (2003). Classical model selection
via simulated annealing. Journal of the Royal Statistical Society,
Series B, vol. 65, part 2, 503-521.

Computationally, its straight forward, as you just need a 'weighting
with DIC' wrapper around various inla()-calls, and then use that mixture
of results to do your inference.

Alternatively, you can weight using the marginal likelihood if you use
proper and meaningful priors.

messages.body_plain:
On 31 January 2012 14:25, Eddie <eddi...@gmail.com> wrote:
> The error message I got was Error in eval(expr, envir, enclos) : could not
> find function "Temperature" due to my code formula = Response ~
> Temperature(model="iid").

Good, that is the error message you should get, and R tries to
understand what you wanted to do. ;-)

> The formula = Response ~ f(Temperature, model="iid") also run smoothly. I
> tried to understand what is the concept behind "pure random effects".

That model says
y_i = a + e_i + eps_i, where both e_i and eps_i are independent
whereas the regression model is
y_i = a + t_i * beta + eps_i, where t_i are the temperatures.

Forget about the "pure random effects" model until you actually want a
model of that type...  The regression models is what you want.

/Finn
